title: Cost guardrails
point: Check budgets before each call, alert on requests that cost a multiple of their usual price, degrade instead of failing, and attribute every dollar to a route, model and customer.
definition: Cost guardrails are runtime controls on spend. They include per-user or per-tenant budgets checked before a call, anomaly alerts, degraded modes when a budget is spent, and cost attribution by route, model and customer.

objective.text: Given a tenant budget and a trailing median cost, specify the pre-call check, the alert threshold, the degraded mode and the attribution tags that would catch a runaway loop.

misconceptions.claim: A monthly invoice review is enough to control model spend.
misconceptions.correction: A runaway loop can spend a month's budget in hours. Budgets must be checked before each call, and anomalies must alert within minutes.

misconceptions.claim: When a budget runs out, the safest response is to return an error.
misconceptions.correction: Step down the degradation ladder instead: a smaller model, fewer steps or exemplar answers only. The user keeps a reduced service and is told which mode they are in.

l1: Give each user or tenant a budget and check it before every model call. Estimate the call's worst-case cost from its input tokens plus its maximum output.
Alert when one request costs a multiple, such as three times, of its route's trailing median. That catches loops and prompt bugs long before the invoice does.
When a budget is spent, degrade rather than fail: a smaller model, exemplar answers only, or queued work. Tag every call with route, model and customer so spend can be attributed.
l2: A call will send 20,000 input tokens with a 2,000-token output cap. At an illustrative $2 and $10 per million, the worst case is $0.04 plus $0.02, or $0.06.
If the tenant has less than $0.06 left, the gateway switches to the degraded mode before the call. A tenant with a $500 monthly budget gets an alert at $400.
A route's trailing median is $0.25 per request, so the alert threshold is $0.75. A $0.90 request fires an alert carrying its trace ID, tenant and model.
l3: Attribution turns a spike into a diagnosis. With every span tagged by route, model, tenant and feature, a spend jump traces to one tenant's loop rather than a vague rise in total cost.
Pair budgets with loop bounds. A per-task cost cap, such as $1, stops a loop that the step bound missed, and it records a typed termination reason.
The degraded mode is a rung on the degradation ladder. Show the user which rung they are on, and record it on every span so quality reports can separate degraded answers.
